title: The Commission Ceiling: Why a Fully Booked Salon Can Still Be a Low-Margin Business
excerpt: Spring racing season and the Christmas function calendar fill every chair in the salon, but a packed column doesn't guarantee a stronger margin once commission is paid.
content:
Spring racing season and the office Christmas function calendar land almost on top of each other, which means hair and beauty salons and day spas across Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria are heading into the busiest run of weeks in the year. Every chair booked, every treatment room full, blow-dries, colour appointments and spray tans stacked back to back from Melbourne Cup week through to the last Friday before Christmas. For a few months the diary looks the way every owner wishes it looked all year round.

The pattern we typically see is that a fully booked column and a stronger bottom line are not automatically the same thing, and the gap between them is easiest to miss in exactly this kind of season, because a full diary looks and feels like proof the business is thriving. Revenue is climbing, the till is busy, and the owner is run off their feet, which usually gets read as a sign the business is doing well.

What is actually happening underneath that full column is a question of which chairs are generating the revenue, and what each of those dollars costs to produce once commission is paid. That is where the real margin story for a salon or day spa usually sits, and it rarely shows up until well after the season has passed and the quieter numbers of January arrive.

The Column Is a Ceiling, Not a Target

Revenue in a hair or beauty business comes down to the same equation as any appointment-based business: the number of productive chair or room hours available in a week, multiplied by what each hour bills on average. A fully booked column during spring racing season and the run into Christmas tells an owner that demand has reached the ceiling for that chair. It says nothing about whether that ceiling is actually high enough to carry the business through the other nine months of the year, or whether the mix of services filling it is the mix that pays best. A column full of blow-dries and spray tans fills the diary fast but rarely carries the same margin as a column full of colour and treatment services, and a workforce capacity and utilisation review is built precisely to separate hours booked from hours actually generating the margin an owner assumes they are banking.

The Commission Scale That Grows Faster Than the Margin

Most salons and day spas pay stylists and therapists on a sliding commission scale, where the percentage paid rises once an individual team member's personal takings pass a threshold, a structure built to retain the senior talent clients book by name. It works well for retention. It has a less visible effect on margin. Once a senior stylist or therapist steps up a commission tier, every additional dollar they bill in a busy season costs the business more than the same dollar billed by a newer team member still on the base tier, so the busiest column in the salon, run by the most booked out person on the team, is often the one carrying the thinnest margin per dollar of revenue, not the thickest. A season like this one, where demand pushes several senior team members past their threshold at the same time, is exactly when that effect compounds across the whole roster at once. This is the kind of question a cost and margin deep dive is built to answer service line by service line and chair by chair, rather than at the single blended number most salons use to read their own results.

The One Line the Column Doesn't Cap

Retail product sales, the take-home colour, the serum, the aftercare range sitting on the front counter, do not compete for a chair or a treatment room, and do not carry a commission scale anywhere near as steep as the service side. A strong retail attach rate during the only few months a year when foot traffic is guaranteed is one of the few levers available to lift margin without adding another hour to an already full column, and it is routinely the most under-managed line on a salon's profit and loss, because it rarely gets tracked with the same discipline as the booking diary.

None of this is a reflection on how hard a team is working through the busiest stretch of the year, which is genuine and worth recognising on its own terms. It is a comment on what the column is actually saying once commission has been paid and the retail line has been counted separately, and that is worth a look while the season is still running rather than once the quieter numbers of January arrive. None of this is something a bookkeeper would usually flag either, since reconciling commission payments accurately is a different job to asking whether the commission structure itself is still serving the margin it was designed around years ago. For an owner past the point of holding that whole picture in their head, a fractional CFO brings exactly that outside read, and a discovery call is a reasonable place to start before the Christmas rush is in full swing.

faqs.q: Why can a fully booked hair or beauty salon still have thin profit margins?
faqs.a: A full column measures demand, not margin. Once commission tiers, product cost and the mix of services filling each chair are accounted for, a fully booked diary can produce less margin than a quieter one with a better service mix. A cost and margin deep dive looks at this chair by chair and service line by service line rather than at one blended revenue number.

faqs.q: How do sliding commission scales affect profitability in Australian salons?
faqs.a: Sliding commission scales reward senior stylists and therapists with a higher percentage once their personal takings pass a threshold, which helps with retention but means each extra dollar they bill in a busy season costs the business more than the same dollar from a team member still on the base tier. Busy seasons can compound this across the whole roster at once.

faqs.q: What is a reasonable commission percentage to pay senior stylists or therapists?
faqs.a: There is no single figure that holds across every salon, because it depends on rent, product cost and the service mix each chair carries. What matters more than the percentage itself is whether the business has modelled what each tier actually costs once it is triggered, rather than setting the scale once and never revisiting it as the team and the season change.

faqs.q: How many chairs or treatment rooms does a salon need to cover its costs?
faqs.a: This depends on rent, wages and the average bill per hour each chair generates, which varies enough between salons that a generic rule of thumb is rarely useful. A workforce capacity and utilisation review builds this number from the business's own figures rather than an industry average.

faqs.q: Why does retail product revenue matter for salon and day spa margin?
faqs.a: Retail sales do not compete for a chair or a treatment room and carry a much lighter commission load than the service side, which makes them one of the few ways to lift margin without adding another hour to an already full column. Busy seasons with guaranteed foot traffic are the best time to lift the attach rate.

faqs.q: When should a hair and beauty business bring in a fractional CFO?
faqs.a: Usually once the owner can no longer hold the full financial picture of commission tiers, retail margin and seasonal cash timing in their head alongside running the floor. A fractional CFO brings that outside structure without replacing the bookkeeper, who continues to handle the day to day ledger and compliance work.
